quote: the two-year-old will ignore the easily accessible toy and go after the apparently forbidden one
content: This is Brehm & Weintraub (1977), a small reactance demonstration whose result was narrower than the retelling suggests: the forbidden-toy preference appeared in the boys and not the girls in the original sample. A single low-N study with a sex interaction is thin support for a universal claim about how desire tracks obtainability. The broader phenomenon (psychological reactance) is real and replicable, but this particular vivid anecdote is the kind of striking-but-fragile demonstration that Influence tends to feature.

quote: they became more opposed to coed dorms
content: The banned-speech effect comes from Worchel, Arnold & Baker (1975, Journal of Applied Social Psychology; no stable DOI), and the "forbidden information becomes more attractive" pattern is genuine but strongly moderated. Reactance to censorship depends on the perceived legitimacy and motives of the censor; when restriction is seen as benevolent or the source as credible, the boomerang shrinks or reverses. The essay presents a one-directional law ("forbidden = more desirable"), whereas the literature describes a conditional effect that can flip with framing, which weakens the claim that this is a fixed feature of the machinery.

quote: The conventional theory for explaining this is
content: Psychological reactance (Brehm 1966) is one of the more durable social-psychology constructs: it has a validated measurement scale (Dillard & Shen 2005) and replicates across persuasion contexts, so crediting it here is fair. The weak link is the next move, the evolutionary gloss that leaping on disappearing options "may be a good adaptation in a hunter-gatherer society." That is an untested just-so story; reactance needs no adaptationist origin tale to be real, and supplying one adds an unfalsifiable layer the data do not support.

Nearly every demonstration in this essay is sourced to Cialdini's Influence, a popular trade book that selects maximally striking findings, several of them decades old, small-sample, or (like the supermarket beef-buyer study) reported as unpublished fieldwork. The scarcity/reactance principle survives scrutiny, but the dramatic magnitudes quoted, six-times-as-much beef, four-thousand-then-thirteen-thousand-dollar jury swings, should be read as memorable illustrations rather than stable effect sizes. Much of mid-century persuasion research was conducted before the methodological reforms that followed social psychology's replication crisis, and point estimates from that era routinely fail to reproduce at their original strength.
